items.title: Wall Street jumps back as Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia CEO
items.content_html:
Nov 23 (Reuters) - US stocks surged on Monday, led by a big jump in the Nasdaq as Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO drove investors back into AI-related shares after last week's rout.

Nvidia's (NVDA.O) shares shot up as much as 36.6% after the board returned Huang. He had resigned from the company on November 12 after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

US President Donald Trump said he secured a deal with Nvidia's board to bring back Huang as CEO. Nvidia is widely seen as a cornerstone of the AI trade.

The news helped Wall Street recover from last week's sharp selloff. On Friday, the S&P 500 and the Dow both confirmed corrections as worries mounted about the AI trade.

The Nasdaq-100 (.NDX) added more than $2 trillion in market value on Monday, while the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 had their biggest daily gains since the market surged after Trump paused his "Liberation Day" tariff package in April 2025.

"The thought had been, and it's being borne out today, that Jensen Huang is uniquely important to Nvidia and to the AI trade," said Thomas Martin, senior portfolio manager at Globalt Investments.

Still, he said, "you have one issue that is resolved -- and it's a biggie -- but you still have to see how the rest of things play out."

According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 (.SPX) gained 328.45 points, or 4.75%, to end at 7,238.84 points, while the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) gained 1,463.21 points, or 6.47%, to 24,080.94. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 1,452.56 points, or 3.02%, to 49,599.89.

Before Monday, the Nasdaq had come close to entering a bear market as investors worried about the heavy borrowing underpinning AI investment and questioned whether the sector could deliver sufficient returns. Fears of political scrutiny also mounted after Democrats swept the US midterm elections.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (.SOX) and S&P 500 information technology sector (.SPLRCT) both were sharply higher on Monday, along with megacap stocks such as Amazon (AMZN.O), Microsoft (MSFT.O), Meta (META.O) and Alphabet (GOOGL.O).

Also climbing were neocloud and data-center companies, which had come under sharp selling pressure following Huang's abrupt exit. Other sectors also rose, with energy (.SPNY) being the only group in negative territory.

"We don't think the rebound has run its course, and at these levels, it's not too late to gradually add back technology exposure," said Andrew Slimmon, senior portfolio manager at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

Ahead this week is Wednesday's personal consumption expenditures report, which could give clues about the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook.

items.title: Kalshi pauses operations in Utah after adverse federal court ruling
items.content_html:
Nov 23 (Reuters) - Kalshi has paused its operations in Utah following an adverse federal court judgment, a spokesperson for the prediction market platform said on Monday.

  • Utah's attorney general brought criminal charges against Kalshi and two of its top executives last month, accusing the company of illegally promoting online gambling and allowing an undercover agent to place sports bets
  • Prediction markets let people wager on the outcome of events such as sports and elections
  • The suspension comes as the federal court has not yet granted an emergency request by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission to block enforcement actions by the state of Utah, according to Kalshi spokesperson
  • Under President Donald Trump's administration, CFTC has backed Kalshi's view that prediction market trading falls exclusively under the jurisdiction of the US derivatives regulator
  • Calling the suspension an "unfortunate outcome" for its Utah-based customers, Kalshi spokesperson said the move affects more than 177,000 users in the state
  • "We will continue to fight this in court, and we look forward to returning to Utah once our legal position is vindicated," the spokesperson said
  • Kalshi has been at the center of an escalating legal battle over the ability of state gaming regulators to police companies in the fast-growing prediction markets industry
  • While several states have battled Kalshi in court, only Arizona has pursued a criminal case, which a federal judge later blocked

Reporting by Anirban Sen in New York and Pritam Biswas in Bengaluru; Editing by Shilpi Majumdar

items.title: Trump saw Nvidia's Huang as protector of open-weight AI models, sources say
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance personally intervened in Nvidia's (NVDA.O) decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang over the weekend, convinced he alone protected American-made open-weight AI models, people familiar with the matter said on Monday.

Open-weight AI models are systems whose core components are publicly available for users to download, modify and adapt for specific tasks. Their growth has become a major business opportunity for Nvidia because they broaden demand for the company's chips and computing infrastructure beyond a handful of large AI developers.

China leads in the development of open-weight AI systems, which are gaining ground with US companies because they can be cheaper than proprietary AI tools from top US labs OpenAI and Anthropic (ANT.O). They can also perform nearly as well.

Nvidia has been one of the most prominent backers of the US open-weight ecosystem. Nvidia in August agreed to buy the company Hugging Face, a platform that developers use to host open-weight AI models, among other AI-related resources. Nvidia is also an investor in Reflection AI, an American company that launched its first open-weight model in October.

Huang and Nvidia's lobbyists have also pressed US lawmakers to support the development of open-weight AI technology, with Huang writing in a letter earlier this year that they should avoid "premature restrictions" on such tools.

Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month following reports that he engaged in several extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Reuters reported on November 18 that the Trump administration was considering requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, including open-weight models, as part of an effort to reduce reliance on Chinese technology.

Republican lawmakers have increasingly echoed the argument that open-weight AI is critical to competing with China. Two leading House Republican lawmakers on Friday called on the Trump administration to help American companies developing open-weight AI models, adding that it would position the US to better counter China.

Reporting by Steve Holland in Washington and Erin Banco in New York; Additional reporting by Courtney Rozen in Washington; Writing by Susan Heavey; Editing by Matthew Lewis

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: US discussing military training for Syrian forces
items.content_html:
• US, allies discuss military training for Syrian forces - sources
  • Plans focus on demining, explosives disposal and border security
  • Syrian reservations over US military access complicate talks - sources
  • US Leahy Laws pose funding hurdles over human rights concerns

DAMASCUS, Nov 23 (Reuters) - The US is discussing plans to train Syrian soldiers in demining, five people familiar with the proposal said, in what would be the first US training mission with the Syrian military since former rebel fighters took power in Damascus in 2024.

The proposal for a multinational training mission still faces legal hurdles in the United States and scepticism among some in the Syrian military, the sources said. But if it moves ahead it could see the US return a small number of troops to Syria as soon as next year, just a year after withdrawing a decade-old mission to fight Islamic State.

Four of the sources said the initial programme would emphasise training in demining and safe disposal of ordnance, but could serve as a model for wider cooperation if successful.

The proposal envisages building on a body known as the Damascus Coordination Center (DCC), set up last year in Jordan to facilitate cooperation between Syrian authorities, American forces and regional allies.

Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for the US military's Central Command, said the DCC was continuing its work in support of a stable, unified and peaceful Syria, and full decisions had not yet been taken on its future structure and mission focus.

A spokesperson for the US State Department said Washington welcomed having a partner in Damascus committed to combating Islamic State. The Syrian Defence Ministry did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

The framework under discussion would also involve personnel from about 15 US allies, including Britain, France, Germany, Australia, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, according to a person involved in the discussions.

RAPPROCHEMENT

Greater military cooperation would be a further step in a rapprochement between Washington and Damascus since the overthrow of President Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.

Washington lifted broad economic sanctions on Syria in December 2025, removed its designation as a state sponsor of terrorism in August 2026, and eased arms-export and defense services restrictions in October, allowing licences to be considered case by case. But there are still hurdles on both sides to direct military cooperation.

In the United States, legislation known as the Leahy Laws prohibits US assistance to foreign security forces' units when there is credible information that they have committed gross violations of human rights.

American officials would need to vet prospective Syrian recipients before providing funding, two of the sources said.

The human rights concerns stem in part from the backgrounds of some commanders in Syria's new security forces, including former members of Islamist armed groups. UN investigators have also documented abuses by forces affiliated with the new authorities.

On the Syrian side, some in Syria's defense ministry have been reluctant to grant American military personnel access to its institutions and facilities, complicating efforts to establish training programmes, the sources said.

During Syria's 2011-2024 civil war, hundreds of US troops were deployed in Syria without cooperating either with Assad's government or the main Sunni Muslim rebel forces that ultimately toppled him. The Americans mainly worked alongside Kurdish forces under Operation Inherent Resolve, a mission to battle Islamic State in both Syria and Iraq.

The last US troops were withdrawn from Syria in April this year and from Iraq in September, although the wider operation has not been fully wound down. Syrian Defence Minister Murhaf Abu Qasra met the operation's commander, Rear Admiral Liam Hulin, in Damascus on November 12, according to Syrian state news agency SANA.

A Syrian military source said the meeting included discussions about the proposed multinational coordination mechanism, plans to train Syrian forces in demining and explosive ordnance disposal, as well as unspecified assistance with border security.

One option under consideration would involve training Syrian soldiers in both Jordan and Syria, potentially beginning in March, with limited US military participation.

The arrangement could also involve the Syrian National Mine Action Centre (SNMAC), a government body responsible for coordinating mine clearance, as a way of facilitating cooperation. The SNMAC did not respond to a request for comment.

US officials are exploring whether remaining funding from Operation Inherent Resolve could support the programme, two of the sources said. One estimated the available funds at approximately $200 million. Reuters could not independently verify the amount.

Reporting by Feras Dalatey in Damascus
Editing by Peter Graff

items.title: US business activity growth eases further in November, survey shows
items.content_html:
Nov 23 (Reuters) - US business activity growth slowed further in November as high prices held back new orders and capacity constraints restrained output, but overall activity remains resilient, suggesting economic growth is continuing at an above-trend rate, a survey showed on Monday.

S&P Global said its flash US Composite PMI Output Index, tracking the manufacturing and services sectors, eased to a four-month low of 54.6 this month from a final reading of 55.9 in October. A reading above 50 indicates expansion in the private sector.

The pace of growth slackened in both manufacturing and the vast services sector, which is responsible for roughly two-thirds of US economic activity. The manufacturing PMI slipped to a three-month low of 54.5 from 54.9 in October, while the services PMI dropped to a four-month low of 54.7 from 56.1 last month.

New business in services slid, while new orders in manufacturing were little changed. Input cost pressures eased but remain elevated and suggest inflation overall will stay well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target.

"Although output growth slowed in November, recent readings have been impressively strong, and the PMI surveys still point to GDP (gross domestic product) rising at an annualized rate of about 3% in the fourth quarter," said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. "Growth also remained encouragingly broad-based across both manufacturing and services, with both sectors also still taking on additional staff in numbers that are indicative of a further strong payroll gain during November."

The US economy grew at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter thanks to ongoing strength in consumer spending and the frenetic artificial intelligence build-out, and employers added a greater-than-expected 165,000 workers to their payrolls in October.

"A key concern is the elevated cost of living and resulting pressures on affordability, and the survey price gauges remain at levels consistent with inflation running well above the Fed's 2% target in the coming months, despite some moderation of the rate of inflation in November," Williamson said. "Supply disruptions, widely linked to global shipping delays, also appear to have become more widespread, adding to firms' concerns about being able to fulfill orders and likely to add further to underlying price pressures in the coming months."

The November 12-20 survey period also dovetailed with a sharp selloff in the US stock market, which has been a key pillar supporting consumer spending, on concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom. It was not clear from the survey data whether that development contributed to the softening in this month's PMI readings.

items.title: US arrears leave chemical weapons watchdog facing budget crisis
items.content_html:
THE HAGUE, Nov 23 (Reuters) - The world's chemical weapons watchdog is facing a budget crisis, largely because of missing payments from the United States, and may have to pause work destroying banned munitions in Syria, according to the agency's new head and an internal document.

The Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons was in a "precarious situation", missing a quarter of its annual €83 million ($91 million) budget, Director-General Sabrina Dallafior told member states in The Hague on Monday.

"In recent weeks, the financial challenge has become particularly acute, with the OPCW's largest payer having thus far not made its full 2026 assessed contribution payment to the organisation," Dallafior said in an email sent to staff late on Friday.

She said operational activities would be paused in December to take stock and revise plans for 2027, including "activities partly funded through voluntary contributions, including capacity-building activities and deployments to Syria."

Dallafior did not name the United States, but Washington has long been by far the biggest donor to the independent agency. Two other sources with knowledge of the matter said the United States had not paid its full dues.

The US embassy in The Hague did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Trump administration has also cut funding to some UN bodies and left many commitments unpaid, demanding reforms and accusing the global body of waste, inefficiency and failing to fulfil its potential to broker peace deals.

The OPCW won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2013 for its work eliminating deadly stockpiles in Syria and other countries.

Since the ousting of former Syrian leader Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, OPCW inspectors and Syrian authorities have discovered large quantities of lethal, previously undeclared chemical weapons and are preparing their destruction, an expensive and time-consuming activity.

As of October, the US had only paid 20% of its €17 million 2026 contribution, Greg Koblentz, a US-based biological and chemical weapons expert, told Reuters.

"Budget cuts that delay the verification and destruction of leftover chemical weapons in Syria create an unnecessary risk to international security," Koblentz said.

"The OPCW's financial woes will also prevent it from undertaking new operations such as investigating Russia's use of chemical weapons against Ukraine and Sudan's production and use of chemical weapons," he added.

The organisation has already exhausted an €8 million reserve, Dallafior told the meeting in The Hague.

($1 = 0.9103 euros)

items.title: Most winnings on Polymarket midterm bets went to top 1% of bettors, report says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - A handful of mostly professional and sophisticated accounts on Polymarket's overseas prediction market netted the vast majority of winnings from bets on congressional races in the US midterm elections, according to research to be published on Monday.

The analysis of Polymarket's overseas platform by the Anti-Corruption Data Collective, a nonprofit research group, also found that Polymarket and rival Kalshi were only about as good as mainstream forecasting models at picking election winners.

Prediction market proponents frequently say they surface unbiased and accurate information by channeling the wisdom of crowds, unlike traditional election polls and forecasting models.

But the finding that sophisticated accounts or "wallets" won at the expense of average traders, while markets did not meaningfully outperform forecasters, undercuts that claim, raising questions of whether election betting offers any net social value, according to the nonprofit research group. Polymarket winnings from US congressional races total roughly $23 million.

"Prediction markets create real risks to election integrity that cannot be ignored, while concentrating the financial rewards on a select few," the report said.

PREDICTION MARKETS DEFEND THEIR VALUE

Kalshi and Polymarket say they have developed advanced systems to detect and prevent misconduct and refer suspicious activity to federal authorities.

Polymarket said on social media that its markets accurately forecast outcomes in 98.4% of races, as of the day before Election Day.

"Prediction markets have become an important source of real-time election information as they bring together the knowledge and insights of informed participants to show the public how likely different outcomes are," a company spokesperson said.

A Kalshi spokesperson referred queries to the company's own post-election analysis, which said its results substantially outperformed most forecast models according to a statistical measure known as a Brier score that compares outcomes to forecast probabilities.

According to the research group's report, traders wagered more than $180 million on congressional races on Polymarket's blockchain-based offshore platform, which is publicly visible on the internet.

Just 819 wallets, including many that are automated or controlled by professional traders, reaped 91% of the winnings, putting them in the top 1%, the research group said.

Underscoring that concentration further, the top 0.1% of wallets, or 82, collected more than half of the winnings, it found. Meanwhile, 99% of wallets that bet on the midterms collectively lost $15 million.

The report identified automated and professional accounts by observing round-the-clock activity, trading volume and breadth of market exposure.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which is fighting in court to shield prediction markets from state oversight, has said the industry's forecasts can generate "informational value" that amounts to a public benefit.

However, the research group's work showed that Kalshi, Polymarket and Polymarket US combined showed an accuracy rate of 91% in US Senate races and 95% for House of Representatives elections, more or less matching an equally weighted average of six election forecast models.

The findings are broadly in line with other assessments of prediction markets' accuracy in the midterms, including by CNBC and the New York Times. The latter found prediction markets only began to outperform the forecasters shortly before Election Day.

"There is little learned exclusively from prediction markets not already captured by one of the high-quality available forecast models," the report said.

Reporting by Douglas Gillison in Washington; editing by Michelle Price and Rod Nickel

items.title: North Carolina win gives Democrats biggest US House majority since early 1990s
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 22 (Reuters) - Democrats have won at least 258 seats in the US House of Representatives after this month's midterm elections, securing the largest majority held by either party in Congress' lower chamber in more than three decades.

Democrats gained their 258th seat in next year's House on Sunday, when North Carolina Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated his Republican opponent, according to the Associated Press. Four races remain uncalled in the House, which has 435 seats.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is expected to become the chamber's first Black speaker, noted the milestone in a social media post.

"House Democrats have just secured the largest majority any party in Congress has held this century," he wrote, adding: "BOOM."

Democrats' landslide electoral victory in the US Senate and House underscored voters' deep frustration with President Donald Trump's stewardship of the economy and his decision to launch a war against Iran in February, which drove gas prices up sharply. In poll after poll, voters expressed anxiety about the cost of living and anger at the way Trump has handled the issue.

Democrats last won 258 seats in 1992 and secured 257 in 2008, according to congressional records. Republican majorities in the House topped out at 247 for the 114th Congress from 2015 to 2017.

While Democrats next year will have the biggest House margin for either party since the early 1990s, some years in the 20th century saw far larger majorities. Democrats held 313 or more seats for much of the 1930s, and exceeded 290 seats in the mid-1960s and late 1970s.

Republicans had their largest House majorities in the 1920s, when they held as many as 302 seats.

Reporting by John Kruzel and Katharine Jackson; Editing by Sergio Non and Paul Simao

attachments.title: US House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) speaks about Democrats reclaiming the majority in the House of Representatives in US midterm elections, during a press conference at the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) in Washington, DC, US, November 4, 2026. REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst

items.title: Trump sees difficulties ahead if Schumer leads Senate
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON/BOSTON, Nov 22 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that it would be difficult for him to work with Senator Chuck Schumer if the Democrat is elected Senate majority leader.

"It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "He failed badly as 'Leader' once before, one of the worst [in] history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again."

Schumer, a New York Democrat, is currently minority leader in the Senate but Democrats next year will take control of both chambers of Congress after sweeping wins in midterm elections earlier this month.

Despite the midterm wins, Schumer faces dissatisfied progressives who say a caucus increasingly shaped by younger, anti-establishment lawmakers needs new leadership.

Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen is making a bid for the Senate leadership, although Schumer has said he has the votes to continue as leader. A closed-door, secret-ballot vote is scheduled for next month.

After the elections, Trump appointed hardline loyalist Stephen Miller to run the White House, suggesting the president will take an even more confrontational approach in his last two years in office. But Trump also has hinted he might work with Democrats on issues such as healthcare.

Speaking on CNN on Sunday, Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan, a Minnesota Democrat, said she supported expanding Medicare to cover all Americans. "If we have to call it TrumpCare in order to get it across the finish line, that's fine by me," she said.

Flanagan said she would support Van Hollen for majority leader. "What we heard from voters is that they were pushing back against the status quo," Flanagan said.

Reporting by Katharine Jackson; Editing by Sergio Non and Susan Fenton

attachments.title: US Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) speaks to the media following a weekly Democratic policy luncheon on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC, US, November 17, 2026. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein

items.title: Schumer led Democrats to big Senate win. Now, some say they need a new leader
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 22 (Reuters) - Chuck Schumer led US Senate Democrats through this month's midterm elections that gave them a decisive 56-seat majority in the 100-seat chamber. Progressives responded with a collective "thank you, next," arguing that Schumer should now make way for a successor.

Critics say Schumer's decades in Washington, his age — he turns 76 on Monday — and his close ties to the party establishment make him ill-suited to lead a Senate Democratic caucus increasingly shaped by younger, anti-establishment lawmakers.

"We write first to thank you," leaders of the populist Working Families Party, which backs like-minded Democratic candidates in elections, said in a November 13 letter to Schumer that called for a generational leadership change.

"If you step aside at the height of a victory you helped secure, you would show voters that the Democratic Party heeded their call for change. The new majority can begin its work united and focused on fighting for the people who elected them," it said.

The top Democrat in the Senate for the past decade, Schumer has projected confidence that his colleagues will choose to keep him as their leader in a secret vote on December 1.

"I will be elected majority leader," Schumer, strongly favored to win, told reporters matter-of-factly last week.

But in the first contested Senate Democratic leadership race since 1994, the New York senator faces a challenge from Senator Chris Van Hollen, 67. While only modestly younger than Schumer, the Maryland senator and his progressive allies outside the Capitol have cast him as an agent of change.

Van Hollen has said the 2026 election results show voters are demanding that the party break with the status quo and adopt a bolder approach that gives new voices, including incoming progressive lawmakers, more influence in the caucus. Democrats seized majorities in both the Senate and House of Representatives from President Donald Trump's fellow Republicans, and formally take control of Congress in January.

'TIME FOR NEW IDEAS'

Van Hollen has run an increasingly public campaign in the leadership contest, though the outcome will be determined in private. At least 16 of the 56 members of the Senate Democratic caucus have publicly committed to backing Schumer, while six have said they will vote for Van Hollen.

"I'm in this to win it," Van Hollen said on Thursday. "That's my goal. I think if we want to move forward on an ambitious agenda like this, we need new leadership. We need to change the culture of the Democratic caucus. People need to have more input. Our new members need to be at the table."

Democrats flipped nine Senate seats in November, including in several states Trump won by double digits in 2024. Many of the incoming freshmen said during their campaigns that they would oppose Schumer for Democratic leader.

"Do I like Chuck Schumer?" asked Senator-elect Troy Jackson of Maine. "He's been great, but I do think it's time for new ideas."

In an interview last week on CNN's "State of the Union," Van Hollen cited a "hunger for change" among Senate Democrats, and said two incoming senators won despite Schumer's efforts to back their primary opponents. Van Hollen criticized Schumer for aligning with powerful pro-Israel and cryptocurrency interests in those races.

PROGRESSIVES BACK VAN HOLLEN

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said Van Hollen stands out because he understands how Washington and the Senate work as a past chair of House and Senate Democrats' respective campaign arms, and he is willing to take risks.

"Those two things are what we need right now, and we need to rethink the way we legislate," El-Sayed said, pointing to Van Hollen's trips to advocate for a wrongly deported migrant and to draw attention to Israel's war in Gaza as examples of his willingness to take risks.

Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia suggested that the leadership fight reflects a healthy discussion within the caucus about its future direction.

"And there's nothing wrong with that," Kaine told Reuters.

Senate Democratic leader is the only unresolved role among Congress' top four positions. House Democrats last week nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker in the next Congress, where John Thune will continue to lead Senate Republicans and Representative Jim Jordan will succeed Speaker Mike Johnson as the top House Republican.

On Sunday, Trump said that it would be difficult for him to work with Schumer, writing on his Truth Social platform that the senator "failed badly as 'Leader' once before, one of the worst (in) history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again."

POTENTIAL PRIMARY CHALLENGE

Schumer is up for reelection in 2028, and losing the leadership race could make him a more vulnerable target, as ambitious Democrats such as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez consider running for his seat. A memo from Ocasio-Cortez's campaign acknowledged she could run for president, Senate or reelection to the House in 2028.

For his part, Schumer has swatted down questions about his future beyond the leadership election.

"I'm focused on 2027 and delivering for the American people," Schumer said on Wednesday.

Reporting by Nolan D. McCaskill; additional reporting by Ross Kerber. Editing by Michael Learmonth, Cynthia Osterman and Will Dunham

attachments.title: US Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) speaks next to Senator Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) during a press conference following a weekly Democrat policy luncheon on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC, US, November 10, 2026. REUTERS/Elizabeth Frantz/File Photo

items.title: Southern California port employers, watchmen union reach tentative deal
items.content_html:
Nov 21 (Reuters) - The Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) employers group at the Los Angeles and Long Beach ports said on Saturday it had reached a tentative agreement with the union for security guards, averting a strike that could have disrupted operations at the two busiest cargo shipping hubs in the US.

The International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 represents 250 security officers, or watchmen, who account for a small fraction of the ports' workforce, but their work is critical because they control access at terminal gates, conduct security patrols and report safety issues.

PMA, which represents terminal owners, said the agreement reached on Saturday was subject to ratification by Local 26 members, and the current contract will be extended pending ratification.

The union did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent outside regular business hours.

The two sides resumed federally mediated negotiations on Friday, two days after the parties broke off talks, with the employers group reporting "little-to-no movement from the union on PMA's proposals."

The PMA said at the time that its offer included a one-time bonus of $3,200 for each union member and a wage proposal that would raise average annual earnings for full-time watchmen from more than $170,000 to $198,000.

The offer also called for maintaining fully employer-paid healthcare for active workers and retirees, valued at more than $62,000 each year, and increased pension benefits up to $93,200 a year for workers with the longest tenure.

Talks between the terminal owners and the union have stretched on for more than a year.

Reporting by Akanksha Khushi in Bengaluru, Steve Gorman and Lisa Baertlein in Los Angeles. Editing by Toby Chopra and Mark Potter

items.title: As e-bike battery fires mount, New York weighs tougher restrictions
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 21 (Reuters) - They lean in apartment hallways, charge overnight in bedrooms and carry many of New York City's delivered meals. Increasingly, they are also a source of fires, linked to aging or inferior batteries.

The deaths of 10 people in two recent New York fires — at least one of them determined to be caused by e-bike batteries — prompted the New York City Council to hold an emergency hearing on Friday on a raft of stricter rules for e-bike storage and battery safety.

The three-hour meeting highlighted growing concerns among city residents about the surge in lithium-ion battery fires, which are up about 70% from a year ago. Among other measures, the proposed legislation would make it a crime to possess or use batteries that do not meet safety standards and would ban storing batteries inside apartments.

It is unclear whether the measures will advance. Officials in Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration, including from the New York City Fire Department, criticized the proposals, saying they would penalize everyday riders and low-income delivery workers.

Fire Department Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said the administration had "significant concerns of unintended consequences that would most heavily impact delivery workers, many of whom are immigrants, with limited English proficiency."

Delivery workers "could face losing their livelihoods and having their lives upended through the confiscation of the device they use every day to make a living," she said.

Lithium-ion battery fires have become an international concern since e-bikes and e-scooters soared in popularity during the COVID-19 pandemic. Many of those batteries are now aging, which fire officials say is likely adding to the number of fires.

Governments have taken different approaches. Britain, for instance, has focused on sellers of batteries and devices that use them.

"Unsafe e-bike and e-scooter batteries pose a serious fire risk, which is why we're strengthening the responsibility of online marketplaces and working with local authorities to remove unsafe products from sale," a British government spokesperson said in response to Reuters questions.

In the United States, the Senate unanimously passed legislation on Thursday sponsored by New York's senators, Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand, that would direct the Consumer Product Safety Commission to set mandatory safety standards for lithium-ion batteries used in e-bikes and other micromobility devices. The commission proposed mandatory safety standards for the batteries in June, after a public meeting in 2023. The House of Representatives has already passed the bill.

A commission staff report published in April found 45 deaths from 2017 to 2024 linked to lithium-ion battery fires involving micromobility devices: 19 tied to e-bikes, 15 to e-scooters and 11 to self-balancing scooters or hoverboards.

The issue is particularly acute in New York, where lithium-ion battery fires have reached a record this year. There were 406 such fires through early November, up from 241 in the same period last year, according to Fire Department figures cited by the City Council.

On October 28, an e-bike battery ignited in an apartment in a public housing project in the Bronx, killing four people including an 11-year-old boy. The e-bike was near the doorway, blocking the family's escape, Bonsignore said at the time.

About a week later, a fire in Sunset Park, a working-class Brooklyn neighborhood, killed six people and injured at least seven. Investigators have not determined the cause, but fire officials said two charred e-bikes were removed from the building and batteries were found in debris.

"The recent building fires in Sunset Park and in the South Bronx, which collectively claimed the lives of 10 New Yorkers, are heartbreaking tragedies that underscore the urgent need for action to prevent further loss of life," City Council Speaker Julie Menin said at the time.

Reporting by Maria Tsvetkova and Nichola Groom; Additional reporting by Barbara Lewis; Editing by William Mallard

items.title: Most new Black Democrats in decades to join US Congress, set to sway policy, party
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 21 (Reuters) - The largest class of new Black Democratic lawmakers in more than 30 years will join the US Congress in January after November's midterm elections despite Republican-led redistricting efforts, according to a Reuters analysis.

The electoral outcome sets up a test of whether increased Black representation can translate into legislative power.

Congress will include 13 new Black Democratic members, the largest cohort since 1993, House historian data showed. Four are 34 years old or younger, and more than half of Black House members were first seated in 2021 or later.

The influx of Black lawmakers could reshape Congress' legislative priorities on voting rights, healthcare affordability and economic inequality, while giving a new generation of leaders a greater voice in shaping Democratic policy, political observers say. But the lawmakers' influence will depend on whether they can translate their growing numbers into powerful committee assignments and legislative victories at a time when longstanding civil rights protections face mounting challenges.

Black candidates won 58 seats in the 435-member House for the 120th Congress, down from 61 in the current Congress, with two additional Black candidates in Louisiana headed to December 12 runoffs. Four Black Republicans will depart Congress, leaving US Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina as the only Black Republican in either chamber. Black representation in the Senate reached a record seven members following the election of Democrat Juliana Stratton in Illinois and the upset victory by Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom.

The shift in representation echoes the 1990s, when efforts to expand Black political representation helped usher in a new generation of lawmakers — many of whom have since gained seniority and influence, said Dedrick Asante-Muhammad, president of the Joint Center for Political and Economic Studies.

"This points to how important it was for a significant increase in Black representatives and how it pays off 20 to 30 years later," Asante-Muhammad said.

DIVERSE REPRESENTATION

In 1993, 16 first-time Black members joined when Congress convened, and 17 had joined by the end, the most of any Congress. Five of the current six longest-serving Black House members were first seated in 1991 or 1993.

"When you have proportional representation in Congress, it does allow for diverse representation across committees. Part of the reason why the Congressional Black Caucus formed is so that they could convince leadership to put Blacks on key committees," said Andra Gillespie, a professor at Emory University who studies African American leadership in politics.

All current members of the caucus are Democrats.

"We're all being contacted by our constituents who are impressing upon us the need to be very bold in our approach ... to address what are crises in communities across the country," said caucus chair, US Representative Yvette Clarke, a New York Democrat, citing the affordability crisis as its members' main concern.

REDRAWN MAPS

Four districts held by Black Democrats were among those that Republican-led legislatures redrew to try to gain seats, in a push that intensified after the Supreme Court's April ruling that weakened the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Republicans have flipped none of the three decided so far.

Democrats Shomari Figures and Don Davis won reelection to the House in Alabama and North Carolina, respectively, while Democrat Leticia Gutierrez, who does not identify as Black, won a redrawn district in Texas previously held by Democrat Al Green.

Two Black women have a chance to secure Louisiana's remaining two congressional seats. In a majority-Black Louisiana district redrawn in May, Democrat Chauna Banks will face Republican Blake Miguez in a December 12 runoff. In a neighboring district, Democrat Patricia Moore, who led a nine-candidate field with nearly 18% of the vote, will take on Republican Gabe Firment, who received 17.2%.

US Senator Raphael Warnock, a Georgia Democrat and the 11th Black senator in US history, told Reuters lawmakers must begin shaping their policy agenda before Congress convenes in January. Warnock donated to and campaigned for Colom, who will be Mississippi's first Black senator in more than 140 years.

"I'm focused on ending this war, ending these tariffs, and restoring tax credits that will bring people's healthcare costs down," Warnock said.

Most major legislation will still require bipartisan support in the Senate, and Republican President Donald Trump can veto bills passed by Congress.

NEW FACES, SENIOR LEADERS AND A TEST FOR DEMOCRATS

Black Democrats' leverage will depend on a delegation that is newer, and in some cases much younger, than in the last Congress. Melat Kiros, 29, is the first woman from Gen Z — the generation born between the late 1990s and the early 2010s — elected to Congress and the first Black woman to represent Colorado. She is one of four first-time Black House members who are 34 or younger, alongside Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York and Adrian Boafo of Maryland, both 32, and Donavan McKinney of Michigan, 34. In contrast, the Democratic caucus' senior Black leaders include US Representatives Maxine Waters of California, 88, and Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, 78.

"I'm unapologetically progressive. So many people are looking for bold leadership and I think that too often the messages that come out are that boldness is risky," said reelected US Representative Summer Lee, a Black Pennsylvania Democrat.

The generational mix will be tested at the top, where US Representative Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat and the favorite to become House speaker, would manage a caucus that includes moderates and progressives seeking to move the party beyond its established leadership.

"Democratic leadership is in for some trouble. (Senate Democratic leader Chuck) Schumer and Jeffries are really going to have to push back against what is going to be and has already proven to be a groundswell against their leadership," said Periloux Peay, a political science professor at the University of Maryland.

The Congressional Black Caucus will enter the new session with a record 64 members, up from 62. Chair Clarke said she is focused on aligning progressives and moderates and expressed confidence in Jeffries.

"I'm under the impression that he's not tone deaf and that he will lead as the body requires," Clarke said.

items.title: FBI's criminal information database hacked, CNN reports
items.content_html:
Nov 20 (Reuters) - The FBI is investigating a suspected breach of a nationwide database used by federal, state and local law enforcement agencies to share criminal justice information, CNN reported on Friday, citing two people briefed on the investigation.

The apparent compromise of the National Crime Information Center database would mark the second intrusion involving an FBI system in recent months and the latest in a string of cyber incidents that have alarmed US officials over the past week.

The agency did not respond to a request for comment from Reuters.

The FBI database is used by law enforcement agencies nationwide to store and share information on warrants, criminal histories and background checks.

Previous high-profile cyber disruptions over the past week have included a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a nationwide halt to air travel that disrupted more than 18,000 flights.

A September breach by a digital extortion group known as "ShinyHunters" accessed an FBI jobs website, compromising data on current and former FBI employees.

Reporting by Nathan Layne, Costas Pitas and Jasper Ward; Editing by William Mallard and Sergio Non

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: Nvidia's accounting is a focus of US SEC investigation, sources say
items.content_html:
NEW YORK/WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The US Securities and Exchange Commission is probing Nvidia's accounting practices, said two people briefed on the matter, adding to the legal woes facing the scandal-hit chip giant.

The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday reported that the SEC was probing Nvidia but said it could not ascertain the focus of the investigation. The people, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential issues, said SEC enforcement staff are scrutinizing potential accounting issues at the company.

A spokesperson for the SEC declined to comment. Spokespeople for Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Prices of Nvidia shares extended losses and were down about 13% on Friday, according to LSEG data, after Reuters reported details of the SEC probe. They had been down more than 6% before Reuters published its report.

Reuters could not immediately determine when the SEC opened its inquiry or exactly what potential accounting issues the watchdog is examining. Investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and many close without resulting in enforcement action.

Still, the accounting focus of the probe, which Reuters is reporting for the first time, increases pressure on Nvidia, whose investors are still reeling from revelations about ousted CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital relationships, including with Alice Huang, who US authorities suspect is a Chinese spy. China has denied she is a spy.

Alice Huang led Singapore-based Megaspeed, historically a large Nvidia chip customer, people familiar with the matter have said. US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over possible violations of export controls related to alleged shipments of Nvidia AI chips to China, the US Justice and Commerce departments said this week.

The crisis has sent shares in Nvidia, a linchpin of the AI boom, tumbling more than a third and stoked calls in Washington for tougher action on tech threats posed by Beijing.

Megaspeed has said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and that it conducted "lawful business." Reuters has not been able to reach Alice Huang. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair in a November 8 statement following the reports of his relationship with Alice Huang, without referring to her by name.

The SEC probe is the latest of Nvidia's legal woes. The Justice Department has also been reviewing Nvidia's $12.9-billion deal to buy open-source platform Hugging Face alongside a broader antitrust investigation into the company's acquisitions and practices, Reuters reported last month.

SINGAPORE ACCOUNTING CHANGE BACK IN FOCUS

Last year, Nvidia changed how it reports geographic revenue, using customer headquarters rather than billing addresses, which it said would better reflect the geographic profile of its revenue. The change resulted in Singapore being removed from its geographical breakdown.

The Financial Times, citing company accounts, reported on Tuesday that Nvidia had made the change even as Singapore sales soared to almost half its global revenue.

That accounting shift has drawn renewed press scrutiny in the wake of the Alice Huang scandal.

Southeast Asia has become a hub for chip smuggling to China since the Biden administration barred advanced AI chip exports to that country over concerns they could boost Beijing's military.

Analysts and investors have also grown increasingly concerned about circular AI financing deals, in which chipmakers including Nvidia have pursued complex financial arrangements to help customers fund purchases of their chips and the construction of costly AI infrastructure, such as data centers. Nvidia has backed AI companies and cloud providers and provided guarantees connected to data-center projects that use its equipment.

Critics say such arrangements can make it harder for investors to assess the quality of chipmakers' revenue and their true financial exposure. Speaking to Reuters last month, SEC enforcement chief David Woodcock said the agency was examining AI companies' corporate disclosures to ensure issuers are giving investors the full picture on potential risks.

On its Tuesday earnings call, Nvidia's interim CEO and former CFO Colette Kress said the company was proud of its role in supporting the AI industry, but would be far more selective moving forward about AI industry financing deals.

The SEC under President Donald Trump has pulled back on enforcement, saying it will focus on bread-and-butter securities fraud, including accounting violations that have long been a mainstay of its enforcement work. It recently launched a new financial reporting and accounting unit within its enforcement division, aimed at developing cases in accounting and auditing areas.

(This story has been refiled to correct Nvidia's RIC in paragraph 1.)

Reporting by Chris Prentice in New York and Alexandra Alper in Washington; Additional reporting by Karen Freifeld and Jody Godoy in New York; Editing by Michelle Price and Daniel Wallis

items.title: Texas prisoner moans in pain for minutes during unusual lethal injection, witnesses say
items.content_html:
Nov 20 (Reuters) - A condemned Texas prisoner moaned and yelled out in pain and remained conscious for several minutes after prison officials began administering lethal injections in what witnesses described on Friday as an unusually protracted execution.

Prison officials took about 34 minutes to successfully insert two intravenous lines in convicted murderer Reinaldo Dennes: one in his neck and the other in his left foot after the veins in his arms were found unviable, according to the Texas Department of Criminal Justice.

They began injecting pentobarbital, a caustic barbiturate, at 6:52 p.m. on Thursday, and he was declared dead 15 minutes later, according to the department's records, during which a media witness and a spiritual adviser said Dennes repeatedly moaned in pain.

The spiritual adviser, the Rev. Jeff Hood, recalled Dennes using repeated expletives and saying: "My leg is killing me," and, "My leg it's on fire, it's on fire."

"He was clearly in tremendous distress," Hood, who was inside the execution chamber with his hand on Dennes' shoulder, told reporters. "Twice he said 'it's not working, it's not working, it's not going how it's supposed to go.'"

Hood, who has witnessed 13 executions by lethal injection, told reporters he had not previously seen "anyone able to make complete sentences past 30 seconds."

Public scrutiny of the decades-old execution method has been renewed after Christa Pike, convicted of murder, survived Tennessee's attempt to execute her using pentobarbital in September, leaving her badly injured and unconscious for several days.

And it comes as newly elected Democratic politicians take over some Texas offices in January in what had long been a Republican stronghold, including Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect, who says she opposes capital punishment.

Hood said four or five minutes passed before Dennes' breathing began to slow to heavy gurgling and snoring sounds and he appeared to lose consciousness.

Amanda Hernandez, a spokesperson for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice, said the execution followed Texas protocol, from his being strapped to the gurney at 6:04 p.m. to the declaration of death at 7:07 p.m., just over an hour later.

"It was not a botched execution, it proceeded as planned and it was successful," she said in an interview.

Michael Graczyk, an Associated Press journalist who has been a media witness at nearly 500 executions since the 1980s, said the execution of Dennes was "dramatically different."

He said that Dennes, convicted of murdering diamond wholesaler Janos Szucs during a robbery in 1996, moaned of "excruciating pain." He said that over about three minutes, Dennes, a Christian, repeatedly called out: "Take me, Father! Take me into your arms."

Reporting by Jonathan Allen in New York; editing by Paul Thomasch and Rosalba O'Brien
